**Designed for** someone with intermediate knowledge of R and RStudio. The first
two modules exist to prepare you for this one — if you are comfortable reading a
file, wrangling it with [dplyr](module2.qmd) and drawing a `ggplot2` figure, you
are ready.

Modules 1 and 2 asked *what does the data look like?* This module asks the next
question: **is a pattern we can see in the sample likely to be real in the
population, or could it just be noise?** That is the whole job of inferential
statistics.

## From description to inference

A **descriptive** statistic summarises the sample in front of you: baseline
height averaged 1.55 m, boys were taller than girls by a couple of centimetres.
An **inferential** statistic asks whether that gap would survive if you could
measure every child in the country, not just the 500 in this file.

Three ideas carry the whole session:

- **The null hypothesis.** We start by assuming there is *no* effect — no
  difference between groups, no relationship between variables — and ask how
  surprising our data would be if that were true.
- **The p-value.** How surprising, exactly. A p-value below 0.05 is the usual
  (arbitrary, conventional) line for calling a result "statistically
  significant" and rejecting the null. It is *not* the probability the result is
  real, and a tiny p-value on a trivial effect is still a trivial effect.
- **The effect size.** How *big* the effect is, on a scale that does not depend
  on sample size. A p-value tells you whether an effect is there; an effect size
  tells you whether it matters. **Report both.** Every template below does.

Which test you reach for depends entirely on the *shape* of your question —
specifically, what kind of variables you are relating:

| Your question | The variables | The test |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Do **two groups** differ on a number? | 1 categorical (2 levels) + 1 continuous | **t-test** |
| Do **three or more groups** differ on a number? | 1 categorical (3+ levels) + 1 continuous | **ANOVA** |
| Does one number **predict** another? | 2 continuous | **linear regression** |
| Are **two categories** related? | 2 categorical | **chi-squared** |

: {tbl-colwidths="[40,35,25]"}

Most of this page is three worked **templates** — t-test, ANOVA and regression —
that you can download, point at your own variables, and adapt into a
poster-worthy analysis. The fourth, chi-squared, lives on its
[own deep-dive page](module3-chi-squared.qmd).

::: {.callout-important}
Module 3 is a **prerequisite for [Module 4](module4.qmd)**, the hands-on project
session. There you will take one of these templates and build it into a
*proto-poster* — so the work you do here is the work you present there.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Before you start
Download the dataset and its dictionaries from the
[dataset page](data.qmd#get-the-files) — `data.RDS`, `data_dictionary.csv` and
`data_dictionary_levels.csv` — into your project's `data/` folder, next to
`abcd-synthetic.csv` from Module 1.

The templates are the live materials for this session. Download whichever you
need and open it in RStudio:

- [`R_Template_t.test.R`](../scripts/module3/R_Template_t.test.R) — two-group t-test
- [`R_Template_ANOVA.R`](../scripts/module3/R_Template_ANOVA.R) — one-way ANOVA
- [`R_Template_regression.R`](../scripts/module3/R_Template_regression.R) — simple linear regression
- [`R_Template_chi.square.R`](../scripts/module3/R_Template_chi.square.R) — chi-squared test of independence

Every chunk on this page is drawn from those files, lightly adapted so it runs
from your project root.
:::

## The data

We work on `data/data.RDS`, the same ABCD-shaped dataset as
[Module 2](module2.qmd) — 500 participants across five annual visits, with coded
variable names and a separate [data dictionary](data.qmd). Two of its properties
shape every analysis on this page:

- **It is longitudinal.** The five rows belonging to one child are *not* five
  independent observations, and neither are two siblings from the same family. A
  hypothesis test assumes independent observations, so we have to engineer that
  independence ourselves (below).
- **About 27% of cells are missing, and the missingness is structured** — never a
  uniform random sprinkle. Dropping incomplete rows is never free; it quietly
  changes *who* you are studying. We use complete cases here because it keeps the
  code readable, but we flag it as a choice, not a default.

## 0. Load libraries

Following the convention from [Module 2](module2.qmd), we load only the two
workhorses — **dplyr** and **ggplot2** — with `library()`. Every function from
another package is written with its package name attached, like `tidyr::drop_na()`
or `car::leveneTest()`, so you can always see at a glance where a function comes
from.

```{r}
#| label: libraries
library(dplyr)    # data wrangling
library(ggplot2)  # figures
```

You will also need these installed —
`install.packages(c("tidyr", "car", "moments", "lmtest"))`: **tidyr** for
`drop_na()` and `pivot_wider()`, **car** for Levene's test, **moments** for
skewness and kurtosis, and **lmtest** for the Breusch-Pagan test.

## Anatomy of a template

All three templates follow the **same seven steps**. Learn the shape once and
every test on this page — and most you will meet later — becomes a matter of
swapping in different variables:

1. **Clean** — pick your variables, keep the baseline visit, give the columns
   readable names, and decide what to do with missing data.
2. **Visualise** the raw variables, before any test.
3. **Check assumptions** — mainly normality and, where it applies, equal
   variances.
4. **Engineer independence** — keep one child per family so siblings do not
   count twice.
5. **Run the test.**
6. **Compute an effect size.**
7. **Visualise the result.**

The three templates differ only in steps 3, 5, 6 and 7 — exactly the steps that
depend on your question. Steps 1, 2 and 4 are nearly identical every time.

# Template 1 · Two groups: the t-test

**The question: do boys and girls differ in height at baseline?** One continuous
outcome (height), one two-level grouping variable (sex). That is the signature of
a **t-test**.

## Clean

We pick five columns, keep only the baseline visit (`ses-00A`), rename the cryptic
ABCD columns, recode sex from `1`/`2` to labels, and drop rows missing any of our
variables.

```{r}
#| label: tt-clean
data <- readRDS("data/data.RDS")

clean <- data |>
  select(
    participant_id,
    session_id,
    family_id = ab_g_stc__design_id__fam,  # needed for the independence step
    sex       = ab_g_stc__cohort_sex,
    height    = ph_y_anthr__height_mean
  ) |>
  filter(session_id == "ses-00A") |>       # baseline only -- no longitudinal modelling here
  mutate(
    sex = case_when(                        # recode the codes...
      sex == 1 ~ "Male",
      sex == 2 ~ "Female",
      .default = NA
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("Female", "Male"))  # ...then make it a factor
  ) |>
  tidyr::drop_na(family_id, sex, height)    # complete-case analysis (a choice, not a default)

glimpse(clean)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Going deeper
Complete-case analysis throws away everyone with a gap. Because ABCD's
missingness is *structured* — see the [dataset page](data.qmd#what-is-missing-and-why) —
that can bias your result. Multiple imputation is the better tool, but it is well
beyond this session; naming the trade-off is what matters here.
:::

## Visualise

Always look before you test.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tt-dist
#| fig-cap: "Baseline height, split by sex"
#| fig-alt: "Two overlaid-then-faceted histograms of baseline height, one panel for females and one for males; both are roughly bell-shaped, with the male panel shifted slightly to taller values."
#| warning: false
ggplot(clean, aes(x = height, fill = sex)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  facet_wrap(~sex) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of baseline height by sex", x = "Height", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Check assumptions

**Normality.** The Shapiro-Wilk test asks whether a sample could have come from a
normal distribution (p > 0.05 is reassuring). Skewness should sit roughly within
±2 and excess kurtosis within ±7. A Q-Q plot shows the same thing by eye — points
hugging the line mean "normal."

```{r}
#| label: tt-normality
clean |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(
    shapiro_p = shapiro.test(height)$p.value,  # p > 0.05 is reassuring
    skew      = moments::skewness(height),     # aim for roughly within +/- 2
    kurtosis  = moments::kurtosis(height)      # moments::kurtosis() centres a normal at 3
  )
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## You will also see `by()`
Base R does the same per-group check with `by()` — it splits a vector by a
grouping factor and applies a function to each piece. You will meet it in older
scripts and other people's code, so it is worth recognising:

```{r}
#| label: tt-normality-base
by(clean$height, clean$sex, shapiro.test)
```

We use `group_by() |> summarise()` on this page because it returns a tidy table
and folds skewness and kurtosis into the same call — but the two give the same
Shapiro-Wilk result.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-tt-qq
#| fig-cap: "Q-Q plot of height by sex"
#| fig-alt: "Quantile-quantile plot of height for each sex; points fall close to the diagonal reference line, indicating approximately normal distributions."
#| warning: false
ggplot(clean, aes(sample = height, color = sex)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  labs(title = "Q-Q plot by sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Equal variances.** A standard t-test assumes the two groups have the same
spread. Levene's test checks it: p > 0.05 means equal variances are a fair
assumption, so we can use `var.equal = TRUE`. If it failed, we would switch to
Welch's correction (`var.equal = FALSE`).

```{r}
#| label: tt-levene
car::leveneTest(height ~ sex, data = clean)
```

## Engineer independence

Siblings share a family, so two children from one family are not independent
observations. We keep a single, randomly chosen child per family. `set.seed()`
makes that random choice reproducible — anyone running the code gets the same
sample.

```{r}
#| label: tt-independence
set.seed(1996)  # any fixed number works; it just has to be the same every run

clean_no_sibs <- clean |>
  group_by(family_id) |>
  slice_sample(n = 1) |>  # one child per family
  ungroup()

nrow(clean) - nrow(clean_no_sibs)  # how many siblings were dropped
```

## Run the t-test

```{r}
#| label: tt-test
t_result <- t.test(height ~ sex, data = clean_no_sibs, var.equal = TRUE)
t_result
```

Read it as: `t` is the test statistic, `df` the degrees of freedom, `p-value`
whether to reject the null of equal means, and the `95% CI` the plausible range
for the true difference. If the interval excludes zero, the groups differ.

## Effect size: Cohen's d

The p-value says *whether* the means differ; Cohen's d says *by how much*, in
standard-deviation units. Rough guide: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.

```{r}
#| label: tt-effect
d <- clean_no_sibs |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(height), sd = sd(height))

pooled_sd <- sqrt(sum((d$n - 1) * d$sd^2) / (sum(d$n) - 2))
cohens_d  <- abs(diff(d$mean)) / pooled_sd
cat("Cohen's d:", round(cohens_d, 3), "\n")
```

## Visualise the result

```{r}
#| label: fig-tt-result
#| fig-cap: "Baseline height by sex"
#| fig-alt: "Boxplots of baseline height for females and males with individual points jittered over them; the male box sits slightly higher, matching the significant t-test."
#| warning: false
ggplot(clean_no_sibs, aes(x = sex, y = height, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = 16) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Baseline height by sex", x = "Sex", y = "Height") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

# Template 2 · Three or more groups: ANOVA

**The question: does baseline height differ across parental-education groups?**
Now the grouping variable has **five** levels, so a t-test will not do — we need a
one-way **ANOVA**, which generalises the t-test to any number of groups.

The cleaning and independence steps are the *same shape* as the t-test, so the
prose is lighter here — watch the pattern repeat.

## Clean

```{r}
#| label: aov-clean
clean <- data |>
  select(
    participant_id,
    session_id,
    family_id    = ab_g_stc__design_id__fam,
    parental_edu = ab_g_dyn__cohort_edu__cgs,  # five ordered levels
    height       = ph_y_anthr__height_mean
  ) |>
  filter(session_id == "ses-00A") |>
  mutate(
    # case_when() recodes; factor(levels = …) fixes the order for plots and post-hoc tests
    parental_edu = case_when(
      parental_edu == 1 ~ "less_than_HS",
      parental_edu == 2 ~ "HS_diploma",
      parental_edu == 3 ~ "some_college",
      parental_edu == 4 ~ "bachelor_degree",
      parental_edu == 5 ~ "graduate_degree",
      .default = NA
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("less_than_HS", "HS_diploma", "some_college",
                        "bachelor_degree", "graduate_degree"))
  ) |>
  tidyr::drop_na(family_id, parental_edu, height)

glimpse(clean)
```

## Visualise

```{r}
#| label: fig-aov-dist
#| fig-cap: "Baseline height across parental-education groups"
#| fig-alt: "Five small histograms of baseline height, one per parental-education group; each is roughly bell-shaped and they overlap heavily."
#| warning: false
ggplot(clean, aes(x = height, fill = parental_edu)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  facet_wrap(~parental_edu) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of height by parental education", x = "Height", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Check assumptions

Same normality battery as before, now *within each of the five groups*, plus
Levene's test across all five. ANOVA is fairly robust to mild non-normality when
groups are reasonably sized.

```{r}
#| label: aov-normality
clean |>
  group_by(parental_edu) |>
  summarise(
    shapiro_p = shapiro.test(height)$p.value,
    skew      = moments::skewness(height),
    kurtosis  = moments::kurtosis(height)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: aov-levene
car::leveneTest(height ~ parental_edu, data = clean)
```

## Engineer independence and run the ANOVA

```{r}
#| label: aov-test
set.seed(1996)
clean_no_sibs <- clean |>
  group_by(family_id) |>
  slice_sample(n = 1) |>
  ungroup()

anova_result <- aov(height ~ parental_edu, data = clean_no_sibs)
summary(anova_result)
```

The `Pr(>F)` column is the p-value. A significant ANOVA tells you *that* at least
one group differs — but **not which one**. (If Levene's test had failed, you would
swap `aov()` for `oneway.test(height ~ parental_edu, var.equal = FALSE)`, Welch's
ANOVA.)

## Post-hoc: which groups differ?

Tukey's HSD compares every pair of groups while correcting for the many
comparisons, so you do not inflate your false-positive rate. Run it **only if the
ANOVA was significant**.

```{r}
#| label: aov-tukey
tukey_result <- TukeyHSD(anova_result)
tukey_result
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-aov-tukey
#| fig-cap: "Tukey HSD: pairwise differences with 95% confidence intervals"
#| fig-alt: "A dot-and-interval plot of every pairwise difference between parental-education groups; intervals crossing the zero line are not significant."
#| fig-height: 7
#| warning: false
plot(tukey_result, las = 1)
```

Any interval that crosses zero is a pair that does **not** differ significantly.

## Effect size: eta-squared

Eta-squared (η²) is the share of total variance in height explained by group
membership. Rough guide: 0.01 small, 0.06 medium, 0.14 large.

```{r}
#| label: aov-effect
anova_summary <- summary(anova_result)
ss_between <- anova_summary[[1]]["parental_edu", "Sum Sq"]
ss_total   <- sum(anova_summary[[1]][, "Sum Sq"])
eta_squared <- ss_between / ss_total
cat("Eta-squared:", round(eta_squared, 3), "\n")
```

## Visualise the result

```{r}
#| label: fig-aov-result
#| fig-cap: "Baseline height across parental-education groups"
#| fig-alt: "Boxplots of baseline height for the five parental-education groups with jittered points; the boxes overlap substantially, matching a small effect size."
#| fig-width: 10
#| warning: false
ggplot(clean_no_sibs, aes(x = parental_edu, y = height, fill = parental_edu)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = 16) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Baseline height across parental-education groups",
       x = "Parental education", y = "Height") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))
```

# Template 3 · Two continuous variables: regression

**The question: does weight predict height at baseline?** Two *continuous*
variables — an outcome (height) and a predictor (weight) — call for **simple
linear regression**, which fits the best straight line through the cloud of
points and tells you how steep and how reliable it is.

## Clean

No recoding this time, since both variables are already numeric.

```{r}
#| label: reg-clean
clean <- data |>
  select(
    participant_id,
    session_id,
    family_id = ab_g_stc__design_id__fam,
    weight    = ph_y_anthr__weight_mean,  # predictor
    height    = ph_y_anthr__height_mean   # outcome
  ) |>
  filter(session_id == "ses-00A") |>
  tidyr::drop_na(family_id, weight, height)

glimpse(clean)
```

## Visualise

For regression, the first look *is* a scatter plot with a fitted line.

```{r}
#| label: fig-reg-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Height against weight, with a fitted line"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of baseline height against weight with an upward-sloping regression line and confidence band; taller children tend to be heavier."
#| warning: false
ggplot(clean, aes(x = weight, y = height)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Height against weight", x = "Weight", y = "Height") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Engineer independence and fit the model

```{r}
#| label: reg-model
set.seed(1996)
clean_no_sibs <- clean |>
  group_by(family_id) |>
  slice_sample(n = 1) |>
  ungroup()

reg_result <- lm(height ~ weight, data = clean_no_sibs)
summary(reg_result)
```

The `weight` row's `Estimate` is the slope — the predicted change in height for a
one-unit rise in weight — and its p-value tests whether that slope differs from
zero. `R-squared` is the share of variation in height the model explains.

## Check assumptions (after fitting)

Regression's assumptions live in the **residuals**, so we check them *after*
fitting: residuals should be normal (Shapiro + Q-Q) and have constant variance
(the Breusch-Pagan test; p > 0.05 is good). The residuals-vs-fitted plot should
look like a flat, shapeless band — no funnel, no curve.

```{r}
#| label: reg-residuals
shapiro.test(residuals(reg_result))  # normality of residuals
lmtest::bptest(reg_result)           # Breusch-Pagan: constant variance?
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-reg-resid
#| fig-cap: "Residuals against fitted values"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of regression residuals against fitted values with a dashed line at zero and a smooth trend; the cloud is roughly flat and even, indicating constant variance."
#| warning: false
ggplot(data.frame(fitted = fitted(reg_result), residuals = residuals(reg_result)),
       aes(x = fitted, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, color = "tomato") +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs. fitted values", x = "Fitted", y = "Residual") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Effect size: R² and standardized beta

For simple regression, `R-squared` *is* the effect size (0.02 small, 0.13 medium,
0.26 large). The standardized beta re-expresses the slope in standard-deviation
units, so it no longer depends on the measurement scale.

```{r}
#| label: reg-effect
r_squared <- summary(reg_result)$r.squared
cat("R-squared:", round(r_squared, 3), "\n")

beta <- coef(reg_result)["weight"] *
  (sd(clean_no_sibs$weight) / sd(clean_no_sibs$height))
cat("Standardized beta:", round(beta, 3), "\n")
```

## Visualise the result

```{r}
#| label: fig-reg-result
#| fig-cap: "Simple linear regression of height on weight"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of height against weight with the fitted regression line and a shaded confidence band rising from lower-left to upper-right."
#| warning: false
ggplot(clean_no_sibs, aes(x = weight, y = height)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "steelblue", fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(title = "Height predicted by weight", x = "Weight", y = "Height") +
  theme_minimal()
```

What if **both** of your variables are categorical — say, income band and whether
a child feels their neighbourhood is safe? Then none of the three tests above
fit, and you want a **chi-squared test of independence**. It has its own template
and its own walk-through:

## Exercise · make a template your own

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise · ~15 min
Pick whichever template matches a question you care about, and swap in your own
variables from the [data dictionary](data.qmd#browse-the-variables). For example:
is there a sex difference in **weight** (t-test)? Does **household income** (three
levels) relate to a cognition score (ANOVA)? Does **screen time** predict a
mental-health score (regression)?

Change only the `select()` block and the variable names — the rest of the
template carries over.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution — weight by sex (t-test)
```{r}
#| label: ex-solution
sol <- data |>
  select(participant_id, session_id,
         family_id = ab_g_stc__design_id__fam,
         sex       = ab_g_stc__cohort_sex,
         weight    = ph_y_anthr__weight_mean) |>
  filter(session_id == "ses-00A") |>
  mutate(sex = case_when(sex == 1 ~ "Male", sex == 2 ~ "Female", .default = NA) |>
           factor(levels = c("Female", "Male"))) |>
  tidyr::drop_na(family_id, sex, weight)

set.seed(1996)
sol_no_sibs <- sol |> group_by(family_id) |> slice_sample(n = 1) |> ungroup()

t.test(weight ~ sex, data = sol_no_sibs, var.equal = TRUE)
```
Only the two variable names changed from Template 1 — that is the whole point of a
template.
:::

## What you can now do

- Match a research question to the right test by looking at the **shape** of its
  variables — two groups, many groups, two numbers, or two categories.
- Clean a longitudinal extract down to one baseline row per family, and say out
  loud what your missing-data choice costs.
- Check the assumptions a test rests on — normality, equal variances,
  independence — instead of assuming them.
- Report an **effect size** alongside the p-value, and read a confidence interval.
- Produce the figure that goes next to the test on a poster.

## Slides & readings

The slides from the live session, plus two short papers that go deeper on the two
judgement calls this module keeps running into — how big an effect has to be to
matter, and what to do about missing rows.

[Download the Module 3 slides (.pdf)](../scripts/module3/Module_3_Lecture.pdf){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}

- [Dick et al. (2021)](../scripts/module3/Dick-et-al-2021-meaningful-associations.pdf) —
  interpreting a **meaningful effect size** at the sample sizes ABCD works at
- [Dong & Peng (2013)](../scripts/module3/Dong-Peng-2013-missing-data-methods.pdf) —
  principled approaches to **missing data**
